# Working on agent-skills

Every skill in this repo must load and work in Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode and the DeepSeek harness, for any user.

## Layout

- `skills/<name>/SKILL.md` is a skill. Bundled files sit next to it in `references/` and `scripts/`.
- `bin/subagent` and `lib/subagent/` are the dispatch CLI. No dependencies; Node 20+.
- `config/tiers.json` holds the default model per harness and tier. `config/profile.example.md` is the template for a user's profile.
- `install.sh` links skills into `~/.claude/skills` and `~/.agents/skills`.
- `scripts/validate.mjs` and `test/` are the checks.

## Rules for a skill

- Frontmatter has only `name` (kebab-case, equal to the folder name) and `description` (1024 characters or fewer). Other fields are not read by every harness.
- The description says what the skill does and when to use it, with the trigger phrases (for example "Use when the user types /name or asks ...").
- Write the body for any harness. When a step needs a harness-specific tool, name the tool for each harness, or give a fallback that works from a shell. `skills/state-of-the-world/SKILL.md` (diagram routes) shows the pattern.
- Write for any user. Personal context (names, projects, internal tools, private paths, report folders) belongs in `~/.config/agent-skills/profile.md`. A skill that needs it says "read the user profile if it exists" and works without it.
- Skills that change things outside the machine (repos, cloud, messages) audit first, show a plan, and act only after the user says yes.
- Refer to bundled files by relative path (`references/x.md`, `scripts/y.mjs`). The validator checks they exist.
- Scripts in skills use Node or Python with no dependencies. Keep the logic that decides pass or fail in pure functions, and test them with fixtures in `test/`.
- Write prose in plain style: follow `skills/explain-style/SKILL.md`.
- No secrets, customer data or private content. Keep your own private-terms list in `~/.config/agent-skills/private-terms.txt` so the validator can catch slips.

## Before you commit

```bash
node scripts/validate.mjs && node --test test/*.test.mjs
```

(`npm run check` runs the same thing.) For a change to `bin/` or `lib/` that affects how a harness is called, also run `subagent doctor --probe`, which sends one short task per harness.

name: cloud-setup
description: Audit and configure cloud projects against a secure, cost-safe baseline. Google Cloud is covered in full, and AWS accounts and Azure subscriptions follow the same method. Checks billing and budgets, enabled APIs, IAM least privilege, service-account keys, public exposure (buckets, firewall rules), audit logs, labels, and keyless CI access from GitHub (workload identity federation). The audit is read-only, then the user approves a plan, then the agent applies it with the cloud CLI or Terraform and audits again. Use when the user types /cloud-setup, or asks to "set up", "configure" or "harden" a GCP project, AWS account or Azure subscription, "create a new cloud project", "add a budget alert", "connect GitHub Actions to GCP", or "review IAM".
---

# Cloud setup

Bring a cloud project to a known, safe baseline, or bootstrap a new one. Cloud changes cost money and can lock people out, so this skill is strict: audit first, show a plan, change only what the user approves, and audit again.

If the user profile exists (`~/.config/agent-skills/profile.md`, see the repo README), read it first. It can name the CLI configuration, organization, billing account, region, labels and budget defaults.

## 0. Pin the target and the identity

- **Which cloud and which project.** Google Cloud project ID, AWS account ID, or Azure subscription ID. Never guess. If the user named none, list what the CLI can see and ask.
- **Which identity.** Show who the CLI acts as before anything else: `gcloud config list` and `gcloud auth list`, `aws sts get-caller-identity`, or `az account show`. Confirm it is the right account for this project.
- **Do not change the user's defaults.** Pass the project explicitly (`--project`, `--profile`, `--subscription`) instead of switching the active configuration. Use a named configuration only if the profile names one.
- **Is it managed as code?** Look for Terraform, Pulumi or deployment config that names this project (`grep -rl <project-id> --include=*.tf .`). If the project is managed as code, make changes in the code and run its plan. Do not fix drift by hand.

## 1. Audit (read-only)

**Google Cloud:**

```bash
node <this skill's folder>/scripts/audit-gcp.mjs <project-id> [--configuration <name>] [--json]
node <this skill's folder>/scripts/audit-gcp.mjs <project-id> --print-commands   # list the read-only gcloud calls, run nothing
```

The script runs read-only `gcloud` commands and checks these:

- the project is active, billing state, and a budget alert that covers the project;
- no `allUsers` or `allAuthenticatedUsers` IAM bindings;
- no Owner or Editor roles on service accounts;
- owners and members from outside domains;
- user-managed service-account keys, and how old they are;
- ingress firewall rules open to the internet on SSH, RDP or all ports;
- public buckets, and buckets without uniform access or public-access prevention;
- data-access audit logs, labels, and the enabled APIs.

Each finding has a suggested `gcloud` fix for you to review. The script never runs those fixes. The `gcloud` launcher is a POSIX shell script. If `/bin/sh` is blocked or broken on the machine, add `--shell bash` to start it through `bash`.

**AWS and Azure:** run the read-only commands in `references/aws-azure.md` and fill the same checklist. Use a cheap-tier worker (the `subagent` skill) to sort long JSON outputs. You read the findings yourself.

Report unknown checks (no permission to read) as unknown, not as a pass.

## 2. Plan

List each finding with its fix, the risk of the fix, and the rollback. Order: public exposure first, then keys and broad roles, then cost guards, then hygiene. Mark the changes that can break something running, for example removing a role a workload uses or closing a firewall rule. Check usage first (recent logins, recent key use, the services that run as that account).

Ask for a clear yes on the plan. Ask separately, naming the consequence, before any of these:

- linking or changing a billing account, or creating a project;
- granting or removing Owner, Editor or any IAM admin role;
- deleting anything (keys, rules, buckets, service accounts, projects);
- changing organization policies or folders;
- enabling paid services or creating resources that bill by the hour.

## 3. Apply

- Run one change at a time, with the project flag set explicitly, and show each command before you run it.
- With Terraform, run `terraform plan`, show the plan, and wait for a yes before `terraform apply`.
- Add before you remove: grant the narrower role first, check the workload still works, then remove the broad one.
- Keep a rollback line for each change (for example, the `add-iam-policy-binding` that undoes a removal).

## 4. Verify and report

Re-run the audit. Report each check before and after, what is still open and why, and the rollback commands. Do not paste key material, tokens or full IAM policies with personal emails into notes or logs.

## New project bootstrap

When the user asks for a new project, follow `references/gcp-bootstrap.md`. It covers: create under the right folder, link billing (with a yes), set a budget with alerts, enable only the APIs needed, add labels, create a deploy service account with narrow roles, and set up workload identity federation, so that GitHub Actions deploys without service-account keys. Pair it with the `github-setup` skill for the repository side.

## Rules

- Read-only until the user says yes. One yes covers the plan you showed, not later additions.
- Never create, download or print service-account keys, access keys or secrets. Prefer workload identity federation and short-lived credentials.
- Never weaken a control to make a check pass, and never remove the user's own access.
- Treat cost as a risk: say when a change can create charges.
- Write the prose in plain style (the `explain-style` skill).

name: explain-codebase
description: Build an interactive, code-grounded tour of a repository (or one subsystem) as an HTML page, with a clickable architecture map, traced end-to-end flows with file:line links, "where do I change X" paths, a glossary and how to run it, pinned to a commit so it can be refreshed. Use when the user types /explain-codebase or /tour, or asks to "explain this codebase", "give me a tour of <repo>", "onboard me / someone to <repo>", "how does <repo> fit together". Not for recent work in this task (use /explain or /state-of-the-world).
---

# Explain a codebase

Produce a tour a new engineer can use to find their way around in an hour. Every claim on it points at real code at a pinned commit. The page is the answer; chat gets the link and a few lines.

## 1. Pin the subject

- **Repo and commit.** Resolve the checkout and the exact commit. Prefer the upstream default branch: `git fetch`, then read from a detached worktree of `origin/<default>` in the scratchpad (`git worktree add --detach <scratch>/<name> origin/main`). Never change the user's checkout to do this. Record the full SHA.
- **Scope.** Whole repo by default. If the repo is large (>~1,500 tracked files) or the user names an area, say which subsystem you cover and list the rest as "not covered".
- **Audience.** Default: an engineer new to this repo. Adjust for FDE/operator (deploy, config, runbooks) or PM/exec (capabilities and boundaries, little code).
- **Gate.** Read the user profile (`~/.config/agent-skills/profile.md`) if it exists and run any repository check it names. Read any repo `AGENTS.md`/`CLAUDE.md`. If the checkout is customer, demo, deployment or experimental (not OSS), the tour stays private and must leave out customer data, secrets and hostnames. Say this when you give the link.

## 2. Gather evidence (read-only)

1. Read the entry docs yourself: README, CONTEXT/INTENT/ARCHITECTURE files, docs index, top-level manifests (package/pyproject/compose/Helm/Makefile/start scripts). These give you the intended shape.
2. Map the tree: `git ls-files | awk -F/ '{print $1"/"$2}' | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn` and the entrypoints (main modules, servers, CLIs, workers, migrations).
3. **Fan out in parallel** with 3–5 read-only, cheap-tier workers (see the `subagent` skill: Explore agents in Claude Code, `spawn_agent` in Codex, or `subagent batch` from any shell), one slice each (for example: backend/API, data model and storage, background workers and integrations, frontend, deploy and config). Ask each for a structured return:
   - components: name, one-line role, key files, entrypoints, what it talks to (with the call site as `path:line`);
   - 1–2 flows that cross its boundary, step by step, each step with `path:line`;
   - terms of art and what they mean in this code;
   - for every claim: `checked` (read the code) or `inferred` (from names/docs).
4. **Pick 2–3 flows** that best explain the system (the main user action end to end, the main background loop, the deploy/startup path). Trace each yourself through the subagent leads until you have read every step.
5. **Verify citations mechanically.** Before writing the page, check that every `path:line` you will cite exists at the pinned SHA and that the line contains the symbol you name (`git show <sha>:<path> | sed -n '<line>p'`, or a short script over all citations). Fix or drop anything that fails. Report how many citations were checked.

## 3. Page structure

Load `explain-style` for all prose. If you will publish with the `Artifact` tool, load `artifact-design` before writing. Sections, in this order:

1. **Header stamp.** Repo, commit SHA (short) and date, scope, audience, and "checked / inferred" legend.
2. **What it is, in one paragraph.** What the system does, for whom, and its main moving parts.
3. **System map (centerpiece).** An inline SVG of the components and their connections, grouped by layer (clients, API, services/workers, storage, external systems). Each node is clickable and opens a side panel: role, key files (links), entrypoints, talks-to, and gotchas. Edge labels name the protocol or call (HTTP, MCP, queue, SQL).
4. **Traced flows.** For each flow, a step-through (Next/Back) that highlights the path on a small diagram and shows, for each step, what happens, the `path:line` link and a 1–5 line excerpt. Use real excerpts; keep each short.
5. **Where do I change X.** A table of 8–12 common tasks (add an API endpoint, add a connector/integration, add a DB column + migration, change a UI page, add a config value, add a test) → files to touch, in order, and the test to run.
6. **Glossary.** Domain terms as the code uses them, each linked to where it is defined.
7. **Run it, test it.** The minimum commands to start it locally and run the tests, taken from the repo (not invented), with prerequisites.
8. **Not covered / open questions.** What the tour skipped and what you could not confirm.

Links: if the repo has a public remote, use permalinks at the pinned SHA (`https://github.com/<org>/<repo>/blob/<sha>/<path>#L<line>`). For private repos, use permalinks too (they work for people with access); never inline large private code.

Code that is not pushed (a local change set): cite repo-relative paths, mark each cited file new / changed / unchanged against the pushed base commit, attach the cited lines (1–5) to every cite so the page opens them in place, and link only unchanged files at the base SHA. Say in a header status note that the change set is not in the repository yet. A change-set tour in the private tours folder (see section 4), if one exists on this machine, is the worked example.

Mark `inferred` items visibly (dashed outline on the map, a small tag in panels). Only `checked` items look solid.

## 4. Publish, keep, refresh

- Publish as a private Artifact where the harness has one (Claude Code: the `Artifact` tool, `icon`: "map"). Otherwise give the absolute path of the built HTML file. Title: "<Repo> Codebase Tour" (or "<Repo> <Subsystem> Tour").
- Keep the generator in the private tours folder, `~/.local/share/agent-skills/explain-codebase/tours/<repo>/`. It is outside the skills repo, so private tours are never committed, and it outlives the session's scratch folder. `install.sh` links `share_lint.py` into `~/.local/share/agent-skills/explain-codebase/`, so tour scripts that import it from two folders up keep working. If a tour already exists there, copy its layout: `data.py` (all content and `path:line` + symbol cites), `verify.py` (checks each cite with `git show <sha>:<path>` against the repo's git objects, so no checkout is needed; set `TOUR_REPO`), `template.html`, `build.py` and `parsecheck.js`. Run verify → build → parsecheck, then publish the built HTML. verify.py and build.py both call `share_lint.py` (see Rules) and fail on a hit. Add the artifact URL to `tours/<repo>/README` line once published.
- **Refresh mode.** When the user asks to refresh a tour, read the existing artifact, take `git diff --stat <old-sha>..<new-sha>`, re-verify every citation at the new SHA, update only the parts the diff touched, and republish to the same URL with a changelog line in the header.
- Reply with the link and 3–5 lines: scope and commit, the flows traced, the citation check result, and anything flagged as inferred or not covered.

## Rules

- **Shareable by default.** Write for someone who has the repository and nothing else. No local paths (`~/`, `/Users/`), personal launchers or instances, loopback ports other than the repo's documented defaults, private output folders, agent or tool names, people's names, or anything learned only from memory or private notes. Define every product, site and domain term in the glossary with a cite. Give run commands from the repo root using the repo's own scripts. `share_lint.py` enforces the mechanical part. Add personal patterns (your launchers, instance names, allowed default ports) to `~/.config/agent-skills/share_lint.json`, tour-specific patterns as `LINT_EXTRA` in data.py, and exact repo strings to allow (for example a default URL in cited code) with `LINT_ALLOW`.

- Read-only on the repo. No builds, installs or test runs are needed for a tour; quote commands, do not run them unless the user asks.
- Never cite a line you did not verify. Never describe intended behaviour (from docs) as actual behaviour (from code) without saying which it is.
- Prefer one accurate map with 10–20 nodes over an exhaustive one. Group small modules.

name: explain-concept
description: Teach one concept (an algorithm, protocol, math idea, ML technique, security mechanism, system design pattern) as an interactive HTML page the user can play with, with an intuition, a diagram, a live widget, a worked example and quick self-check questions. Use when the user types /explain-concept or asks "explain X to me", "help me understand X", "teach me X", "make me an explainer for X". Not for recent work in this task (use /explain) or for a whole codebase (use /explain-codebase).
---

# Explain a concept

Make one throwaway, interactive web page that teaches one idea well. The page is the answer. Chat gets one or two lines and the link.

## 1. Pin the target (no questions unless it is ambiguous)

- **The concept.** Name it in one line. If the ask is broad ("explain transformers"), pick the one idea under it that unlocks the rest (attention) and say so.
- **The reader.** Default: the user. Read the user profile (`~/.config/agent-skills/profile.md`) if it exists; without one, assume a strong engineer who is not a specialist in this topic. Adjust if the user names another audience (a customer, a new hire, an exec).
- **The anchor.** If the concept shows up in the user's own work (the profile may list their projects), use that as the running example. A concept tied to the reader's own system sticks better than a textbook one.
- **The format rung.** Pick the lowest that works and say which:
  - one-paragraph answer → reply in chat in plain style, no page;
  - structure or flow → a diagram (inline widget, or a page with one SVG);
  - something to explore or tune → **interactive page (the default for this skill)**.

## 2. Get it right before making it pretty

- Work out the explanation first, then design. A beautiful wrong page is worse than a plain right one.
- For anything factual, current or version-specific, check sources (docs, papers, the code itself). Cite them on the page with links.
- If the widget computes something (a hash, a gradient step, a scheduling order), run the core function once on a sample input before publishing. The numbers the reader sees must be real.
- Mark simplifications on the page ("This ignores X; that matters when Y").

## 3. Page structure

Load `explain-style` for all prose on the page. If you will publish with the `Artifact` tool, load `artifact-design` before writing (that tool requires it). Then, in this order:

1. **One-sentence answer.** What the concept is and what problem it solves, at the very top.
2. **Intuition.** A concrete analogy or picture, 3–5 sentences. Say where the analogy breaks.
3. **The diagram.** One SVG showing the moving parts and how data or control flows between them. Label with the same terms as the text.
4. **The live widget (the centerpiece).** One thing the reader changes to see the idea work: a slider, a step-through with Next/Back, an editable input, a toggle between two cases. It opens in a meaningful state, not empty. Show the effect next to the control.
5. **Worked example.** One full pass with real values, step by step.
6. **Where it shows up / why it matters.** Tie back to the anchor (the user's system) if there is one. Name the usual failure modes and gotchas.
7. **Check yourself.** Three short questions with click-to-reveal answers. At least one asks the reader to predict what the widget will do.
8. **Go deeper.** 2–4 links to the best sources, plus the related concepts to learn next.

Keep the page to what fits on about three screens before the widget. Cut anything the reader does not need to reach the "aha".

## 4. Publish and hand over

- Publish as a private Artifact where the harness has one (Claude Code: the `Artifact` tool, `icon`: "lightbulb" or similar). Otherwise write one self-contained HTML file (inline CSS, JS and SVG; no build step) to a scratch folder and give its absolute path. Title: the concept's name, e.g. "Raft Leader Election".
- Reply with the link and one line: what the widget lets you try first.
- If the user has a learning-tracker skill (the profile may name it), offer to log the concept there (do not log without a yes).

## Rules

- One concept per page. Offer a second page instead of growing this one.
- Never invent numbers, benchmarks or citations. If unsure, say so on the page.
- No secrets, customer data or private code on a page about a public concept. A page that uses the user's private code as the anchor stays private; say that when you give the link.

name: explain-style
description: Plain-writing rules ("80% of the way to ASD-STE100", Simplified Technical English) for explanations, walkthroughs and docs. Other explain skills load this file for their prose. Use directly when the user asks to rewrite text "in plain style", "in STE", "simpler", or "more readable".
---

# Explain style: 80% STE

ASD-STE100 (Simplified Technical English) is a controlled language from aerospace maintenance manuals. Its rules make text fast to read and hard to misread. We use about 80% of it: the rules below, without the strict approved-word dictionary.

## Sentences

- One idea per sentence. One instruction per sentence.
- Procedure sentences (do this, then that): 20 words or fewer.
- Description sentences (what something is or does): 25 words or fewer.
- Paragraphs: 6 sentences or fewer. Start with the main point.
- Use the active voice. Say who or what does the action: "The worker writes the row", not "The row is written".
- Write instructions in the imperative: "Run `make test`", not "You should run `make test`".
- Use simple tenses (present, past, future). Avoid "would have been", "is being".
- Keep "the", "a" and "this". Do not drop them to save words.

## Words

- Use one term for one thing, every time. If the code calls it a `finding`, do not also call it an "alert", "detection" or "event".
- Define each technical term once, at first use, in a few plain words.
- Use common, short words: "use", not "utilize"; "start", not "initiate"; "about", not "approximately".
- Give each word one meaning. Do not use "run" for "execute" in one place and for "a pipeline run" in another without care.
- No noun stacks longer than three words. "Case template seed migration step" becomes "the step that seeds case templates".
- Technical names (functions, files, products, flags) are allowed as they are. Put code names in backticks.

## What we relax (the other 20%)

- No fixed approved-word list. Domain words are fine when defined.
- Short lists, tables and fragments are fine where they scan better than sentences.
- A reason clause ("because …", "so that …") is fine; it is often the most useful part.
- Tone can be natural. Do not make it robotic.

## Check before you send

- Can a reader who is new to the subject follow each sentence on its own?
- Is the most important fact in the first sentence?
- Did any one term change its name halfway through?
- Is there a sentence over 25 words? Split it.

name: explain
description: Explain recent work in the current agent task when asked for a walkthrough or clarification. Use when the user types /explain or $explain, or asks "walk me through what you did", "why did you do X", or "explain this change".
---

# Explain

Connect the user's goal, the meaningful work, the evidence, and what remains. Treat `$explain` and `/explain` as requests about the current task unless the user names another subject.

Use the conversation and existing artifacts as evidence. Inspect relevant files, diffs, or results read-only when needed; do not rerun commands just to reconstruct activity. Distinguish what was proposed, attempted, completed, and verified.

Lead with what is now true and why it matters. Explain the decisions and causal flow at the depth the user needs. Include file links, command options, failures, tradeoffs, or side effects when they clarify the outcome. A short explanation does not need a section for every tool call or file.

Tie verification to what it proves: a passing component test does not establish an untested user flow. Call out material uncertainty and the next useful step if work remains. Use a compact diagram only when it makes a relationship easier to understand. Avoid canned conclusions and repeated status summaries.

Write the prose in plain style: follow the `explain-style` skill (80% of the way to ASD-STE100).

name: github-setup
description: Audit and configure GitHub repositories, and GitHub Projects boards, against a chosen baseline. Covers visibility, branch rules, merge settings, Actions token permissions, security features (secret scanning, push protection, Dependabot, code scanning) and community files (README, LICENSE, SECURITY.md, CODEOWNERS, dependabot.yml). The audit is read-only, then the user approves a change plan, then the agent applies it with `gh` and audits again. Use when the user types /github-setup, or asks to "set up", "configure" or "harden" a GitHub repo, "add branch protection", "make this repo public-ready", "turn on Dependabot or secret scanning", or "set up a GitHub project board".
---

# GitHub setup

Bring a GitHub repository to a known baseline, with proof. Audit first, change only what the user approves, and audit again at the end.

If the user profile exists (`~/.config/agent-skills/profile.md`, see the repo README), read it first. It can set the default account, baseline, license, commit email and push rules.

## 1. Pin the target

- **Repository.** `owner/name`, from the user or from `git remote get-url origin`. For several repos, run the audit once per repo; a cheap-tier worker (the `subagent` skill) can run the loop and collect the tables.
- **Baseline.** One of `personal-public`, `personal-private` or `team`. `references/baselines.md` says what each one requires. Default: the profile's baseline, else `personal-public` for public repos and `personal-private` for private ones.
- **Who acts.** Show `gh auth status` (account and scopes). Organization repos may need SSO authorization or an org admin. Say so instead of working around it.

## 2. Audit (read-only)

```bash
node <this skill's folder>/scripts/audit.mjs owner/name --baseline personal-public
node <this skill's folder>/scripts/audit.mjs owner/name --baseline team --json   # for tooling
```

The script reads the repo settings, branch rules, Actions permissions, security features and key files through `gh api`. It prints one row per check: pass, fail, unknown (no permission, or the API did not say) or n/a (not available on this plan). Each failed check names its fix: `api` (the script can apply it), `pr` (a file to add through a pull request) or `user` (needs the user's input or an admin).

## 3. Plan

Group the failed and unknown checks:

1. **Settings the script can apply** (`api`): list the check IDs.
2. **Files** (`pr`): README, LICENSE, SECURITY.md, CODEOWNERS, `.github/dependabot.yml`, CI workflows. Draft them on a branch and open a pull request. Never commit them straight to the default branch. `references/baselines.md` has starting templates.
3. **Needs the user** (`user`): description and topics text, features that need a paid plan, organization policies, anything that changes who has access.

Show the plan as a short table and ask for a clear yes. Ask separately, and name the consequence, before any of these:

- changing visibility (public ↔ private);
- archiving, renaming, transferring or deleting a repo;
- removing collaborators, teams or deploy keys;
- force-pushing or rewriting history.

## 4. Apply

```bash
node <this skill's folder>/scripts/audit.mjs owner/name --baseline personal-public --apply delete-branch-on-merge,vulnerability-alerts --dry-run
node <this skill's folder>/scripts/audit.mjs owner/name --baseline personal-public --apply delete-branch-on-merge,vulnerability-alerts
```

Always run `--dry-run` first and show the exact API calls. After the yes, run it without `--dry-run`. The script applies only the IDs you list, then audits again and prints the before and after.

For files, create a branch, commit, push and open a pull request with `gh pr create`. Follow the profile's push rules; without a profile, ask before every push.

## 5. Verify and report

Re-run the audit. Report a table with each check, its status before and after, and anything still open, with who or what it waits on. Link the pull request for file changes.

## Making a repo public

Visibility is the user's decision. Before you recommend it:

## 1. Find the meeting

Search Quill with the script in this skill's folder. Do not search the Quill folder by hand, because the script already knows its layout.

```bash
python3 <this skill's folder>/scripts/quill.py list --query "<person or topic>" --days 30
```

- Add `--on YYYY-MM-DD` when the user gives a day, such as "yesterday".
- Results with `matched_in: title_or_people` come first. A `transcript` match means that the words were said in the meeting. Many meetings have no useful title, so a transcript match can still be the right meeting. Read its transcript to confirm.
- If the user names no meeting, run `list --limit 5` and use the newest meeting that has a transcript.
- If two results could be the meeting, choose the one that best fits the request and name it in your report. Ask only when the choice changes who gets the follow-up.

## 2. Export it

```bash
python3 <this skill's folder>/scripts/quill.py show <id> --root <packet root>
```

The packet root is the folder that the profile names. If the profile names no folder, use `~/meeting-packets`.

The script creates a private dated folder and prints the paths. The folder holds `transcript.md`, and also `notes.md` if Quill has notes for the meeting. Each transcript line has the form `[mm:ss] Speaker: text`. Read these files in full. Do not paste them into your reply.

## 3. Add only the context that the follow-up needs

The transcript shows what was said. Other sources show what was already sent, promised or agreed. Look for:

- The email thread with these people and the calendar invite, through this harness's connectors if it has them.
- Documents that the meeting mentions.
- Other meetings about this topic, before and after this one: `quill.py list --query "<person or topic>"`. A later internal meeting may change what the follow-up can say.
- Agent threads and local files about this project, if the user points to them or the profile names them.

To read another meeting, export it inside the packet folder with `quill.py show <id> --root <packet folder>/context`. Do not export transcripts to temporary folders, because they are private. Cite these meetings by title and time, such as `[Roadmap review 12:34]`.

Stop when the commitments and the draft are supported. If you cannot reach a source, list it under "Not checked" in the packet. Do not guess what it says.

## 4. Write the packet

Write `packet.md` in the meeting folder. Use this structure. "What happened" is required. Leave out any other section that has nothing in it.

```markdown
# <Meeting title>, <date>

**People:** <names, and mark the ones you could not confirm>

## What happened
<the story of the meeting, in short paragraphs> [12:34]

**Next action for the user:** <one sentence>

## Decisions
- <decision> [12:34]

## Commitments
| Who | What | By when | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| <person> | <what they will do> | <date as stated, or "not stated"> | [12:34] |

## Open questions
- <question, and who can answer it> [12:34]

## Artifacts promised
- <document or demo the follow-up needs, and whether it exists yet, with its path or link>

## Not checked
- <source you could not reach, or a fact you could not confirm>

## Left out of the follow-up
- <sensitive or internal point that the draft leaves out on purpose, and why> [12:34]
```

Write "What happened" so that someone who missed the meeting can follow the next conversation about it. Use 100 to 250 words, not counting citations, and fewer for a short call. Say:

- Why the meeting took place and where things stood when it started.
- The main topics in the order they came up, who raised each one, and how each one ended.
- Any pushback, concern, surprise or change of plan, and who said it. These often do not appear in the lists below.

Write it as a story, not as a list of outcomes. Explain why a decision happened, and leave the full detail to the lists below. Do not add your opinion of the meeting.

Cite each item with a transcript time, a note heading, or a link. A statement with no source goes under "Open questions" or "Not checked". Record a commitment only if someone said it. Do not turn a suggestion or a passing idea into a commitment.

- Follow the writing rules in the profile if it has them. Otherwise keep it short and plain.
- Say what happened and what comes next. Do not recap the whole meeting.
- Include only facts from the packet. Check each name, number, date and promise against its source.
- Do not reveal internal notes or material that the meeting did not share with these recipients.
- Do not repeat a person's candid remarks in writing. Their employer may read that address. Do not name other customers. List what you left out in the packet.

Do not send, post or share anything. Create an email draft if the user asked for one, or if the profile says to create drafts without asking. Use the account that the follow-up will come from. If a connector reaches only a different account, do not create the draft there, and say so. Never send a draft.

Open your report with what happened in the meeting, in two to four sentences. Then give the next action, anything the user must confirm before sending, and the folder path.

# Security review

Find real, reachable weaknesses in code the user owns or is authorized to assess. Report each one with evidence and a fix. A short list of verified findings is worth more than a long list of guesses.

This skill uses the `subagent` skill for delegation. Load it now and follow its brief, tier and checking rules.

## 0. Scope and gate

- **Target.** One of: a diff or PR (quick), a repo or subsystem (standard), or a repo plus threat model (deep). Default: quick for a diff or PR, standard for a repo.
- **Pin it.** Record the repo, branch and full commit SHA. Review a detached worktree of that commit in a scratch folder, not the user's working checkout.
- **Authorization.** Only code and systems the user owns or is authorized to test. Do not scan, probe or attack live third-party hosts. Run code only locally, in a scratch environment.
- **Context gate.** Read the user profile (`~/.config/agent-skills/profile.md`) if it exists. If it names a check to run before a review (for example a repository classification script), run it on the checkout. Read the repo's `AGENTS.md`. For customer, deployment or private checkouts, the report stays private, and briefs go only to the providers the profile allows (by default, the provider of this session or local models).
- **Say the plan.** Before a fan-out, tell the user the mode, the slices, and roughly how many workers at which tiers.

## 1. Deterministic scanners (no model)

```bash
node <this skill's folder>/scripts/scanners.mjs <checkout> --out <run folder> [--offline]
```

The script finds installed scanners (gitleaks, trufflehog, semgrep, osv-scanner, npm audit, pip-audit, bandit, trivy, govulncheck, zizmor, hadolint), runs each read-only, and writes `scanners.json` with what ran, what was skipped and what is missing. `--offline` skips tools that call the network. It never installs anything. If key scanners are missing, list them in the report and offer the install command; do not install without a yes.

Scanner hits are leads, not findings. They go through the same check as model findings (step 4).

## 2. Map the attack surface (cheap tier, parallel)

Split the code into 3 to 6 slices (for example: API and auth, data and storage, background jobs and integrations, frontend, CI and deploy config). Send one cheap-tier worker per slice with a read-only brief. Ask each for a JSON list of:

- entry points: HTTP routes, CLI commands, queue consumers, webhooks, MCP tools, file or URL inputs, with `path:line` and the auth check (or `none`);
- trust boundaries: where untrusted data enters and where privilege changes;
- sinks: SQL, shell or `exec`, templates, file paths, outbound HTTP, deserialization, `eval`, crypto, secrets reads;
- each item tagged "checked" or "inferred".

Merge the maps yourself. This is the input for the hunt and the "checked areas" list in the report.

For a quick (diff) review, skip the full map: map only the entry points and sinks that the diff touches or reaches.

## 3. Hunt (standard tier, one worker per category or component)

Use the categories and the questions in `references/hunt-categories.md`: access control, injection, secrets and crypto, input handling and deserialization, SSRF and outbound calls, supply chain and CI, config and infrastructure, and LLM or agent risks (prompt injection that reaches tools, tool scope, MCP exposure).

Each brief carries the merged map for its area, the scanner leads in that area, and this output contract for each candidate:

```json
{"title": "", "category": "", "location": "path:line", "source_to_sink": ["path:line: what happens"],
 "preconditions": "", "impact": "", "confidence": "high|medium|low", "fix": "", "evidence": "checked|inferred"}
```

Workers describe a weakness in prose. They do not write working exploit code or payloads beyond the minimum needed to name the bug class.

## 4. Verify (frontier tier, other model family)

Every candidate goes to a skeptic whose job is to disprove it. Use a different model family from the one that found it: `subagent batch` with `"via": "other"` and `"tier": "frontier"`, one line per candidate (or per small group in the same file). The skeptic answers:

- Is the input really attacker-controlled on this path?
- Is there a guard upstream or downstream (auth middleware, validation, ORM parameters, framework escaping)?
- Is the code reachable in a real deployment (not dead, not test-only, not behind an admin-only flag)?
- What is the realistic impact?

Verdicts: **CONFIRMED** (evidence holds), **PLAUSIBLE** (could not rule it out; say what would settle it), **REJECTED** (with the reason). Read the key lines yourself for every CONFIRMED finding of high or critical severity. If the two families disagree, report the finding as PLAUSIBLE with both views. Drop REJECTED items, but count them in the report.

In deep mode, also verify the high-impact "checked and clean" claims from step 2 with a second worker. Absence of findings is a claim too.

## 5. Report

Use `references/report-template.md`. Severity = reachability × impact, with one line of reasoning per finding (Critical, High, Medium, Low, Info). For each finding: location, the source-to-sink path, why it is exploitable (prose, no weaponized payload), the fix, verification status, and which models agreed.

Also list:

- areas checked and found clean, with what "checked" covered;
- what was not covered (and why), and which scanners were missing;
- the worker ledger from the `subagent` skill (workers, tiers, models, checked or not).

Save the report in a private place, not inside the reviewed repo unless the user asks: the profile's report folder if it names one, otherwise `~/security-reviews/<repo>-<short-sha>-<date>.md`. Show the findings table and the path in chat.

## 6. Fix mode (only when the user asks)

Fix in a scratch worktree, one finding per commit, each with a test that fails before the fix and passes after. Then re-run step 4 on the changed code. Never push; publication follows the user's normal rules (see the profile).

## Rules

- Defensive work only. No attacks on systems the user does not own, no live-target scanning, no detection-evasion help, no working exploits.
- Redact secrets you find: show the type, the location and the first 4 characters only. Never copy a secret into a brief, a report or a log.
- Undisclosed vulnerabilities stay private. Do not open public issues, PRs or posts about them; the user decides on disclosure.
- Any log, note or status update names the review and the counts, not the exploit details.
- Write the prose in plain style (the `explain-style` skill).

# State of the World

`/explain` looks back at what was just done. This skill looks at the **whole piece of work**, from the first ask to the finished goal, and works out what still has to happen to get there. It uses the same evidence discipline as `/explain`, applied to the full arc instead of the last step.

The subject is the work this thread is about, not only this conversation. If the work began before this session (an earlier session, a context summary, a memory file, a handoff note, open PRs), include that history. If the user names another subject (a project, a PR, an earlier session), use that instead.

## 1. Gather the evidence

- **Find the full scope.** Reread the whole thread, including any context summary. Then follow what it points to: relevant memory files, handoff or plan `.md` files, the repo's branches and PRs, inbox notes. The start of the work is the original problem, not the first message of this session.
- **Treat the conversation and existing artifacts as the evidence.** Inspect files, diffs, PR states and results read-only where they settle a status you would otherwise guess (`git status`, `git log`, `gh pr view`, whether a file exists). Do not rerun builds or tests to reconstruct what happened. Report the last known result and when it was.
- **Keep four states apart for every item:** proposed, attempted, completed, verified. Only verified work is green. Code that is written but untested is in progress. Work that "should work" but was never seen working is unverified. A step that waits on the user, a reviewer or access is blocked, and you say who or what it waits on.
- **Tie each verification to what it proves.** A passing unit test does not prove an untested user flow. A green CI run on one branch says nothing about the branch that has not been rebased. When the proof is narrower than the claim, the item stays amber.

## 2. Restate the goal and the problem (goes first)

In your own words, not the user's:

- **What I think you're trying to achieve.** The end outcome, in one to three sentences. Aim at the real goal behind the work. "Get PR #X merged" is a step. "Stop fresh Helm installs from silently losing tables" is the goal.
- **The problem underneath.** What is broken, missing or painful, and why it matters to the user and to the people they serve.
- **What I'm unsure about.** Any part of the intent you inferred rather than heard. Put it as a short question the user can correct.

## 3. Show the diagram

Render the diagram so the user actually sees it. A Mermaid code block shown as text does not count.

Use the first route that this harness has:

1. **Inline widget** (preferred; Claude Code desktop): call `mcp__visualize__read_me` with the `diagram` module silently, then `mcp__visualize__show_widget` with an SVG flow chart.
2. **Published page** (Claude Code: the `Artifact` tool): write one HTML page with inline SVG to the scratch folder and publish it. Load `artifact-design` first, as that tool requires. Give the link.
3. **File** (any harness): write one self-contained `.html` (inline SVG) or `.svg` file to the scratch folder. Show it with the harness's file tool if it has one (Claude Code: `SendUserFile` with `display: "render"`), and always give the absolute path so the user can open it.

What goes in the diagram:

- A flow from **Start** (the original problem) through the steps and branches to **Goal**, left to right, or top to bottom if it is long. Include the steps still needed to reach the goal, not just those already taken.
- One node per meaningful piece of work, labelled in a few plain words, with a short reference where it helps (PR number, file, command).
- Color every node by status, the same way every time:
  - **Green**: done and verified
  - **Yellow / amber**: in progress, or done but unverified
  - **Red**: blocked or failing, with a short "why" under the label
  - **Gray, dashed outline**: not started
  - **Blue outline** (optional): a decision point or open question
- Include a legend, and mark "you are here" at the current frontier.
- Draw dependencies as arrows. If order matters (A must merge before B), the arrows show it. Abandoned approaches can appear as a faded side branch if they explain the current route.
- Keep it to about 15 nodes. Group minor steps. Make it readable in light and dark themes (use the widget's CSS variables, or colors that keep contrast on both).

## 4. The written summary (after the diagram)

Lead with what is now true and why it matters, at the depth the user needs. Keep it scannable:

- **Where we started.** The original problem and the starting state, in two or three lines.
- **What exists now.** Each completed item with its evidence (file link, PR, command result), and a note on anything unverified.
- **How we got here.** Only the decisions and turns that shaped the path: why this approach, what failed and changed direction, the tradeoffs accepted, the side effects created. Skip anything that doesn't help explain the current state.
- **What's left.** An ordered list of what must still happen to reach the goal, most useful next action first. For each blocked item, name who or what unblocks it.
- **Risks and loose ends** (only if there are any): material uncertainty, stale assumptions, and things dropped along the way.

## Rules

- Write all prose in plain style: follow the `explain-style` skill (80% of the way to ASD-STE100).
- Report only what the evidence supports. Never promote "proposed" to "done". If a status is unclear, color it amber and say why.
- This skill takes stock. It does not do the remaining work. End with the top next step in one line.
- Don't list every tool call or file, and don't repeat the transcript. Avoid canned conclusions and restating the same status twice. The user wants the picture, not the minutes.

# Subagent

You are the lead. You keep the judgment, the integration and the final check. Workers on cheaper models do bounded pieces. This skill says what to hand off, at which tier, how to brief it, how to run it in this harness or another one, and how to check what comes back.

If the user gives a task with /subagent, do that task with this method. If the user gives no task, run the harness check (section 5) and report what is available.

If the user profile exists (`~/.config/agent-skills/profile.md`, see the repo README), read it first. It can set data rules and local conventions that apply to every worker.

## 1. Split the work

**Keep for yourself:** decisions and tradeoffs, anything that needs the whole conversation, combining results, the final check, anything that touches secrets, messages to people, and pushes or deploys.

**Delegate:** work that a stranger could do from a written brief, with output you can check cheaply. For example:

- find, read and summarize code, docs or logs;
- inventories (endpoints, dependencies, config keys, call sites);
- mechanical edits from an exact spec;
- running tests or linters and sorting the failures;
- per-file or per-item checks that fan out;
- drafting tests or boilerplate to a clear spec;
- an independent second opinion.

Do not delegate when the brief costs more than the work, or when you cannot check the result. Run independent pieces in parallel. Run dependent pieces in order, and check A before B starts.

## 2. Pick the tier

| Tier | Claude | Codex | Local (Ollama) | Use for |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| cheap | claude-haiku-5-5 | gpt-6-luna, low effort | qwen3.5 | search, read, summarize, extract, classify, inventory, log triage, mechanical edits with a checker |
| standard | claude-sonnet-5-5 | gpt-6.1-sol, medium | qwen3-coder | scoped code changes, writing tests, debugging with a repro, per-finding analysis |
| frontier | claude-opus-5-5 | gpt-6-astra, high | qwen3.8:27b | design, unclear bugs, security verification, a task a lower tier failed |

`subagent tiers` prints the current table from `config/tiers.json`. If it differs from the table above, it wins.

- Start at the lowest tier that can do the job.
- If a worker fails, sharpen the brief once. If it fails again, go up one tier.
- Never check work with a weaker model than the one that did it. The check is yours, or a tier at least as strong.

## 3. Write the brief

A worker starts with nothing. It has not seen this conversation. Use the template in `references/brief-template.md`:

- **Goal:** one sentence, what and why.
- **Scope:** files, folders, commit; what is out of scope.
- **Constraints:** read-only or write; which files may change; time or cost limit.
- **What you already know:** so the worker does not find it again.
- **Output contract:** the exact format (headings or a JSON shape), `path:line` for every claim, "checked" or "inferred" on each claim, and what to say if blocked.
- **Done when:** the stop condition.

Give each brief one job. Ten small briefs are better than one big one: they run in parallel and fail one at a time.

## 4. Run it

Use this harness's own subagent tool when it has one. The UI shows the workers, and the results come back into your context. Use the `subagent` CLI when you need another model family, a tier this harness does not have, or a run record on disk.

**Claude Code.** Use the Agent tool with `model: "haiku"`, `"sonnet"` or `"opus"` from the tier. These are aliases: in Claude Code 2.1.283 `haiku` resolves to Haiku 4.5 and `sonnet` to Sonnet 5, not the current 5.5 models. That is still cheaper than you; when the exact model matters, use `subagent run --via claude`, which passes exact IDs. Use `subagent_type: "Explore"` for read-only search. Several Agent calls in one message run in parallel. Use `run_in_background: true` for long jobs and `isolation: "worktree"` for workers that edit. For more than about 5 workers or a multi-stage pipeline, use the Workflow tool if this session has it: The user typing /subagent is the opt-in. Keep it under 10 workers unless the user asks for more, and say the size before you start.

**Codex.** Use `spawn_agent` with `model` and `reasoning_effort` from the tier (for example `gpt-6-luna`, `low`). The user typing /subagent is the explicit request that lets you set `model`. Collect results with `wait_agent`. Call `close_agent` when a worker is done, because finished workers still count toward the concurrency limit.

**OpenCode.** Use the task tool with a subagent, or an `@name` mention. The model comes from the agent's file in `~/.config/opencode/agents/`.

**DeepSeek harness.** Use its subagent tool. The model is the profile default.

**Any harness with a shell.** Use the `subagent` CLI (on `PATH` after `install.sh`; the source is `bin/subagent` in this repo):

```bash
subagent run --via codex --tier cheap --cwd <repo> --prompt-file brief.md
subagent run --via other --tier frontier --cwd <repo> --prompt-file review.md
subagent run --via ollama --attach build.log --prompt "List each distinct error with its first line number."
subagent batch tasks.jsonl --parallel 4
```

- `--via other` picks a different model family from yours (Codex when you are Claude, Claude otherwise).
- The answer goes to stdout. The run folder (brief, output, logs, `meta.json` with model, time and cost) is named on stderr.
- `--dry-run` prints the exact command and spends nothing.
- Write tasks need `--mode write --cwd <scratch worktree>`.
- Ollama has no tools. Give it what it needs with `--attach`.
- `--attach` inlines text files with 1-based line numbers (`cat -n` style), so line references in the answer match the file. Pass `--line-numbers=false` to inline the plain text.
- The batch file format is in `references/brief-template.md`.

**Sandboxes.** A harness that runs commands in a sandbox usually blocks the network and keychain that another harness needs. Run `subagent` with this harness's sandbox override (in Claude Code, `dangerouslyDisableSandbox: true` on that Bash call; in Codex, ask for escalation). Say that you did it. Run long jobs in the background and carry on.

## 5. Check which harnesses work

```bash
subagent doctor          # installed, signed in, tier models, where the data goes, skills linked
subagent doctor --probe  # also sends a one-line brief to each harness on its cheap tier
```

Run `--probe` before you rely on another harness in a session, and when the user asks which harnesses work. Show the table. Do not use a harness that fails the probe; say why (not signed in, server down, model not pulled). `references/harness-matrix.md` has the headless commands, skill folders and known traps for each harness.

## 6. Use other harnesses for testing

- **Second opinion.** Send the same review brief with `--via other`. Agreement raises confidence. Disagreement goes to the user with both views. Different model families make different mistakes.
- **Skill or instruction changes.** Write the test brief once and put one line per harness in a batch file. Compare the answers. For example, ask each harness to list the skills it can see.
- **Clean-room setup test.** A write-mode worker in a scratch worktree follows the README install and test steps exactly as written and reports where it got stuck. This finds missing steps.
- **Big local inputs.** Ollama summarizes large logs or files you attach, and no data leaves the machine.

## 7. Check what comes back

A worker's output is a claim, not a fact.

- Open a sample of the cited `path:line` yourself. Open all of them when the result drives a decision.
- Re-run tests that a worker says pass. For write tasks, read the full diff before you take anything from the worktree.
- If the output is wrong or vague, fix the brief and rerun, or go up a tier. Do not hide the gap.
- When you report to the user, say which parts came from workers and what you checked.

## 8. Safety

- Read-only by default. Writes happen only in a scratch git worktree or a folder made for the task. Never in the user's main checkout. Workers never push, publish or deploy.
- A brief is data sent to that harness's provider: Claude to Anthropic, Codex to OpenAI, Ollama stays local, OpenCode goes to its model's provider, and the DeepSeek harness goes to the provider in its profile. Treat free or preview models as public: assume prompts are kept.
- Never put credentials, keys or customer data in a brief. Confidential code goes only to providers the user already uses for that repo (the profile may list them), or to local models.
- Workers do not run session-start rituals from global agent instructions, claim tasks, write logs or notes, or message people. The lead does that once for the whole job. The CLI's worker preamble says this.
- Workers do not start their own workers unless the brief says so. Maximum depth is 2.
- Before a fan-out of more than about 5 workers, say how many and which tiers. Use `--budget-usd` on Claude CLI runs that could loop.

## 9. Report

End with a short ledger: each worker, its tier and model, what it did, the result, and whether you checked it. Then give the combined answer. Write the prose in plain style (the `explain-style` skill).

# agent-skills

Agent skills that work in every local agent harness: Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode and the DeepSeek harness. There is one copy of each skill, and `install.sh` links it into the folders each harness reads. The repo also ships `subagent`, a small CLI that runs a task through any installed harness on a cheap, standard or frontier model.

## Skills

| Skill | Use it for |
|---|---|
| `subagent` | Hand bounded work to cheaper models and run it in parallel. Use the other harnesses as workers, second opinions or test runners, and check which ones work. |
| `security` | Defensive review of a diff, repo, dependencies or config. Scanners run first, then cheap models map the code, a stronger model hunts, and a different model family tries to disprove each finding. |
| `github-setup` | Audit a GitHub repo against a baseline (`personal-public`, `personal-private`, `team`) and apply the fixes you approve: branch rules, security features, Actions token, community files. Also sets up GitHub Projects boards. |
| `cloud-setup` | Audit a Google Cloud project (AWS and Azure by checklist) for budgets, IAM, keys, public exposure and logging, and bootstrap new projects with keyless GitHub Actions access. |
| `learn-later` | Queue topics you want to learn about, then get a 10-minute reading pack for each: a plain brief, SVG diagrams, key terms, a worked example, dated sources and self-check questions. Plain Markdown in a folder you pick once (an Obsidian vault works as is). |
| `meeting-packet` | Turn a recorded meeting into a summary of what happened, commitments, open questions and a draft follow-up, all with sources. Reads Quill's local database, or works from a pasted transcript. It never sends anything. |
| `explain` | Explain recent work in the current task. |
| `state-of-the-world` | Take stock of a whole piece of work, with a color-coded flow diagram from the start to the goal. |
| `explain-concept` | Teach one concept as an interactive page. |
| `explain-codebase` | Build a code-grounded, citation-checked tour of a repo. |
| `explain-style` | The plain-writing rules the other skills use ("80% of ASD-STE100"). |

Invoke a skill with `/name` in Claude Code and the DeepSeek harness, and with `$name` in Codex. OpenCode picks skills by their description.

Every skill that changes something outside your machine is read-only by default. It audits, shows a plan, and changes only what you approve.

## Install

Requires Node 20 or newer. There are no dependencies.

```bash
gh repo clone ShmalexM/agent-skills ~/code/agent-skills
~/code/agent-skills/install.sh --dry-run   # show what would change
~/code/agent-skills/install.sh
subagent doctor --probe
```

`install.sh` links each skill into two folders, which together cover every harness:

| Folder | Read by |
|---|---|
| `~/.claude/skills/` | Claude Code, OpenCode |
| `~/.agents/skills/` | Codex, OpenCode, DeepSeek harness |

The installer also does three other things:

- It puts `subagent` in `~/.local/bin`.
- It moves copies with the same names out of `~/.codex/skills`, because Codex reads both folders and would show them twice.
- It links `share_lint.py` into `~/.local/share/agent-skills/explain-codebase/`, where your codebase tours live outside this repo.

Anything it replaces goes to `~/.local/share/agent-skills/backups/<time>/`; nothing is deleted. `install.sh --uninstall` removes only the links that point into this repo.

The harness folders are links to your checkout, so an edit shows up the next time a harness loads the skill. Restart a harness to see a newly added skill.

# AWS and Azure: read-only audit commands

Run these, read the JSON, and fill the same checklist as the Google Cloud audit. All commands only read. Add `--profile NAME` (AWS) or `--subscription ID` (Azure) instead of changing the user's defaults.

## AWS account

| Check | Command | Fails when |
|---|---|---|
| Identity | `aws sts get-caller-identity` | not the account the user named |
| Root MFA | `aws iam get-account-summary --query 'SummaryMap.AccountMFAEnabled'` | `0` |
| Root access keys | `aws iam get-account-summary --query 'SummaryMap.AccountAccessKeysPresent'` | `1` |
| IAM users with long-lived keys | `aws iam list-users`, then `aws iam list-access-keys --user-name USER` | active keys, especially older than 90 days |
| Admin policies | `aws iam list-entities-for-policy --policy-arn arn:aws:iam::aws:policy/AdministratorAccess` | users or roles that do not need it |
| Budgets | `aws budgets describe-budgets --account-id ACCOUNT` | no budget with notifications |
| CloudTrail | `aws cloudtrail describe-trails` and `aws cloudtrail get-trail-status --name TRAIL` | no multi-region trail that is logging |
| S3 public access block | `aws s3control get-public-access-block --account-id ACCOUNT` | any setting `false` or no configuration |
| Open admin ports | `aws ec2 describe-security-groups --filters Name=ip-permission.cidr,Values=0.0.0.0/0 --query 'SecurityGroups[].{id:GroupId,perms:IpPermissions}'` | port 22, 3389 or all traffic open to `0.0.0.0/0` |
| GuardDuty | `aws guardduty list-detectors` | empty in a region you use |
| GitHub OIDC | `aws iam list-open-id-connect-providers`, then the deploy role's trust policy (`aws iam get-role --role-name ROLE`) | long-lived keys used for CI, or a trust policy without a `token.actions.githubusercontent.com:sub` condition for one repository |

Regional services (security groups, GuardDuty) need a check per region in use: `aws ec2 describe-regions --query 'Regions[].RegionName'`.

| Check | Command | Fails when |
|---|---|---|
| Identity | `az account show` | not the subscription the user named |
| Owners | `az role assignment list --role Owner --scope /subscriptions/SUB --include-inherited` | more owners than needed, or guest accounts |
| Budgets | `az consumption budget list --subscription SUB` | no budget |

## 1. Create the project

```bash
gcloud projects create PROJECT PARENT --labels=env=dev,owner=TEAM_OR_USER
gcloud projects describe PROJECT --format='value(projectNumber)'   # note PROJECT_NUMBER
```

## 2. Link billing (separate yes; this starts charges)

```bash
gcloud billing projects link PROJECT --billing-account=BILLING
```

## 3. Budget with alerts

```bash
gcloud billing budgets create --billing-account=BILLING \
  --display-name="PROJECT monthly" --budget-amount=AMOUNT_USD \
  --filter-projects=projects/PROJECT_NUMBER \
  --threshold-rule=percent=0.5 --threshold-rule=percent=0.9 --threshold-rule=percent=1.0
```

Budgets alert; they do not stop spending. Say so.

## 4. Enable only the APIs needed

```bash
gcloud services enable run.googleapis.com artifactregistry.googleapis.com secretmanager.googleapis.com \
  iamcredentials.googleapis.com sts.googleapis.com --project=PROJECT
```

Adjust the list to the workload. `iamcredentials` and `sts` are needed for step 6.

## 5. Deploy service account with narrow roles

```bash
gcloud iam service-accounts create deployer --display-name="CI deployer" --project=PROJECT
# Example for Cloud Run from Artifact Registry; grant only what the deploy needs.
gcloud projects add-iam-policy-binding PROJECT --member=serviceAccount:deployer@PROJECT.iam.gserviceaccount.com --role=roles/run.admin
gcloud projects add-iam-policy-binding PROJECT --member=serviceAccount:deployer@PROJECT.iam.gserviceaccount.com --role=roles/artifactregistry.writer
gcloud iam service-accounts add-iam-policy-binding RUNTIME_SA@PROJECT.iam.gserviceaccount.com \
  --member=serviceAccount:deployer@PROJECT.iam.gserviceaccount.com --role=roles/iam.serviceAccountUser --project=PROJECT
```

Do not create keys for this account.

## 6. Keyless GitHub Actions access (workload identity federation)

```bash
gcloud iam workload-identity-pools create github --location=global --display-name="GitHub Actions" --project=PROJECT
gcloud iam workload-identity-pools providers create-oidc github --location=global --workload-identity-pool=github \
  --issuer-uri=https://token.actions.githubusercontent.com \
  --attribute-mapping="google.subject=assertion.sub,attribute.repository=assertion.repository,attribute.ref=assertion.ref" \
  --attribute-condition="assertion.repository=='OWNER/REPO'" --project=PROJECT
gcloud iam service-accounts add-iam-policy-binding deployer@PROJECT.iam.gserviceaccount.com --role=roles/iam.workloadIdentityUser \
  --member="principalSet://iam.googleapis.com/projects/PROJECT_NUMBER/locations/global/workloadIdentityPools/github/attribute.repository/OWNER/REPO" \
  --project=PROJECT
```

The attribute condition limits the pool to one repository. To limit it further to the default branch, add `&& assertion.ref=='refs/heads/main'`.

On the GitHub side (with the `github-setup` skill), store these as repository **variables**; they are not secrets:

```bash
gh variable set GCP_WIF_PROVIDER --repo OWNER/REPO --body "projects/PROJECT_NUMBER/locations/global/workloadIdentityPools/github/providers/github"
gh variable set GCP_DEPLOY_SA --repo OWNER/REPO --body "deployer@PROJECT.iam.gserviceaccount.com"
```

The workflow needs `permissions: id-token: write` and the `google-github-actions/auth` action, pinned to a commit SHA, with `workload_identity_provider` and `service_account` taken from those variables.

Pack diagrams are hand-written SVG files, saved next to the pack and embedded with `![alt](file.svg)`. They must read well in light and dark themes, on a phone and on a laptop, in Obsidian, GitHub and a browser.

## Rules

- **Self-contained.** No external images, fonts, scripts or CSS files. Use `font-family="system-ui, -apple-system, Segoe UI, sans-serif"`.
- **Own background.** Draw a full-size `<rect>` with a light fill (`#ffffff` or `#f8fafc`) and rounded corners first. Notes apps in dark mode then still show dark text on a light card.
- **Size.** `viewBox` about 720 wide by 300 to 520 tall, with `width="720"`. No content within 16 px of the edge.
- **Text.** 14 to 16 px for labels, 18 to 20 px bold for the title, and dark text (`#0f172a`). No text under 12 px. Keep labels to 1 to 4 words, and use the same terms as the pack.
- **Color.** 3 to 4 colors at most, each with a meaning, for example:
  - blue `#2563eb` for the main flow;
  - green `#16a34a` for money or value in;
  - orange `#ea580c` for risk or failure;
  - gray `#64748b` for supporting parts.
  Fill boxes with a light tint of the color (for example `#dbeafe`) and stroke them with the full color.
- **Arrows.** Define one `<marker>` arrowhead in `<defs>` and reuse it. Label an arrow when the label explains the step ("pays $100", "mints 100 tokens").
- **Accessible.** Add `<title>` and `<desc>` as the first children of `<svg>`, and add `role="img"` on the root. The alt text in the Markdown says what the diagram shows.
- **Valid XML.** Escape `&` as `&` and `<` as `<` in text. `queue.mjs check` parses every embedded SVG.

## Diagram types that usually help

| Type | Use it for | Shape |
|---|---|---|
| How it works | a mechanism or loop | 4 to 7 boxes left to right, numbered arrows, an optional return path |
| Landscape | types, players or options | a 2×2 grid, or 3 to 5 columns with one example each |
| Timeline | how something got here | a horizontal line with 4 to 8 dated events |
| Before and after | what changes | two panels side by side with the same layout |

# Hunt categories

One worker per category (or per category and component). Paste the relevant block into the brief. Each block lists the questions to answer and the sinks to search for. Search patterns are starting points; read the code around every hit.

## Access control

- Does every entry point from the map check who the caller is (authentication) and what they may do (authorization)?
- Object-level checks: when a handler loads a record by ID, does it check the record belongs to the caller's user, tenant or org? (IDOR)
- Are admin, debug, health, metrics and internal routes reachable without auth?
- Do background jobs, webhooks and MCP tools run with more privilege than the caller who triggered them?
- Search: route decorators, `@router.`, `app.get(`, `permission`, `is_admin`, `tenant_id`, `org_id`, `owner_id`, `get_current_user`, `Depends(`.

## Injection

- SQL: raw strings or f-strings into `execute(`, `text(`, `raw(`, `.query(`; ORDER BY or LIMIT built from input.
- Shell: `subprocess` with `shell=True`, `os.system`, `exec(`, `child_process.exec`, backticks, `bash -c` with interpolation.
- Templates: user input into template source (`render_template_string`, `Template(`, `new Function(`), or HTML without escaping (`dangerouslySetInnerHTML`, `|safe`, `v-html`, `innerHTML`).
- Paths: user input in file paths without normalization and a base-folder check (`open(`, `send_file`, `path.join(` with `..`); archive extraction (zip slip).
- Query languages: LDAP, XPath, NoSQL operators (`$where`, `$regex`), search DSLs, log queries built from input.

## Secrets and crypto

- Hardcoded keys, tokens, passwords, private keys, connection strings (also in tests, fixtures, notebooks, `.env.example` with real values, CI files).
- Secrets written to logs, error messages, traces, analytics or API responses.
- Weak or misused crypto: MD5 or SHA1 for passwords, no salt, ECB mode, static IVs, `random` instead of `secrets`, JWT `alg: none` or no signature check, missing token expiry.
- TLS checks off: `verify=False`, `rejectUnauthorized: false`, `InsecureSkipVerify`.

## Input handling and deserialization

- Unsafe deserialization: `pickle.loads`, `yaml.load` without SafeLoader, `marshal`, Java or .NET binary serializers, `node-serialize`.
- Mass assignment: request bodies mapped straight onto models (role, is_admin, tenant fields).
- Missing size and count limits: uploads, JSON bodies, regexes open to catastrophic backtracking (ReDoS), pagination without a maximum.
- File uploads: type checked by extension only, stored under a guessable public path, served with the user's content type.

## SSRF and outbound calls

- Does any code fetch a URL, host or IP that comes from the user, a webhook, a document or a model output?
- Is there an allow-list, and does it block redirects to internal addresses, cloud metadata (169.254.169.254), localhost and private ranges after DNS resolution?
- Search: `requests.get(`, `httpx`, `fetch(`, `axios`, `urlopen`, `curl`, webhook URL fields, "import from URL" features.

## Supply chain and CI

- Dependencies with known vulnerabilities (scanner output), unpinned versions, install scripts from unknown packages, dependency confusion (internal names resolvable on public registries).
- GitHub Actions: `pull_request_target` with a checkout of the PR head, `${{ github.event.* }}` interpolated into `run:` (script injection), actions pinned to tags instead of SHAs, `permissions:` broader than needed, secrets exposed to forked PRs.
- Docker: running as root, `latest` tags, secrets in build args or layers, `curl | sh` in builds.

## Config and infrastructure

- Helm, Kubernetes, Terraform, compose: privileged containers, host paths, host network, broad RBAC or IAM (`*` actions), public buckets, open security groups, missing network policies, default passwords.
- App config: debug mode on, permissive CORS (`*` with credentials), missing security headers, cookies without `Secure`/`HttpOnly`/`SameSite`, CSRF protection off.
- Services bound to `0.0.0.0` that should be local only.

## LLM and agent risks

- Prompt injection: can untrusted text (tickets, emails, logs, web pages, documents, tool output) reach a model that can call tools with side effects? Trace from the untrusted source to each tool.
- Tool scope: do agent tools run with the user's privileges or more? Can a tool read or write outside its intended scope (arbitrary file paths, arbitrary SQL, arbitrary URLs)?
- Approval gates: which actions run without a human approval, and can model output change what gets approved?
- Model output used as code or commands: `eval`, shell, SQL or file paths built from model output.
- MCP servers: exposed on a network port without auth, tools with broad side effects, secrets passed through tool arguments or results.
- Data leaks: secrets or customer data placed in prompts sent to third-party models, or kept in logs and traces.

## Batch files (`subagent batch tasks.jsonl`)

One JSON object per line. Lines starting with `//` are comments. Relative paths resolve from the batch file's folder. Every line is checked before any task runs.

Keys: `id`, `via` (claude, codex, opencode, ollama, dsh, other), `tier`, `model`, `effort`, `mode` (read or write), `cwd`, `prompt` or `prompt_file`, `attach` (array), `lineNumbers` (default true), `timeout` (seconds), `label`, `budgetUsd`, `raw`, `allowUnsandboxed`.

```jsonl
// same review brief, two model families
{"id": "review-claude", "via": "claude", "tier": "standard", "cwd": "../repo", "prompt_file": "review.md"}
{"id": "review-codex", "via": "codex", "tier": "standard", "cwd": "../repo", "prompt_file": "review.md"}
// local summary of a big log, nothing leaves the machine
{"id": "log-summary", "via": "ollama", "attach": ["ci.log"], "prompt": "List each distinct failure with its first line number."}
```

The batch folder holds one run folder per task and `batch.json` with every task's status, model, time, cost and output path.

# Harness matrix

How each local harness finds skills, runs headless, spawns its own subagents, and where it trips. Checked on 2026-10-12 against Claude Code 2.1.283, Codex CLI 0.158.0, OpenCode 1.18.32, Ollama 0.33.0 and the DeepSeek harness (dsh) from the npx cache. Re-check with `subagent doctor --probe` after upgrades.

| | Claude Code | Codex | OpenCode | DeepSeek harness | Ollama |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Skill folders (user) | `~/.claude/skills` | `~/.agents/skills`, `$CODEX_HOME/skills` | `~/.config/opencode/skills`, plus `~/.claude/skills` and `~/.agents/skills` | `~/.dsh/skills`, `~/.agents/skills` | none (no tools) |
| Invoke a skill | `/name` | `$name` or by description | by description (skill tool) | `/name` or by description | n/a |
| Native subagents | Agent tool (`model`, `subagent_type`, `isolation: "worktree"`), Workflow tool | `spawn_agent` (`model`, `reasoning_effort`), `wait_agent`, `close_agent` | task tool, agent files with `mode: subagent` | subagent tool | none |
| Headless command | `claude -p` | `codex exec` | `opencode run` | `dsh --profile headless "<task>"` | HTTP `POST /api/generate` |
| Read-only switch | `--permission-mode dontAsk` + read-only `--allowedTools` | `-s read-only` | `--agent plan` | none | always (no tools) |
| Model switch | `--model claude-haiku-5-5` (exact IDs; aliases lag) | `-m <slug>` + `-c model_reasoning_effort="low"` | `-m provider/model` | profile default only | `model` field |
| Signed-in check | `claude auth status` (JSON) | `codex login status` | `opencode auth list` | `~/.dsh/settings.yaml` | `GET /api/tags` |

`install.sh` links every skill into `~/.claude/skills` and `~/.agents/skills`. Those two folders cover all five harnesses. It also removes stale copies from `~/.codex/skills`, because Codex reads both folders and would show a skill twice.

## Traps

- **Nested sandboxes.** Inside Claude Code's sandbox, `codex exec` cannot reach its backend and `claude -p` cannot read the keychain. Run cross-harness calls with the sandbox override. Codex's own sandbox (`-s read-only`) still applies to what Codex does.
- **Nested Claude.** Claude Code sets `CLAUDECODE` in its children. The CLI strips it so `claude -p` starts cleanly.
- **Claude aliases lag.** `--model haiku` runs Haiku 4.5 and `--model sonnet` runs Sonnet 5 in Claude Code 2.1.283. The tiers use exact IDs (`claude-haiku-5-5`, `claude-sonnet-5-5`, `claude-opus-5-5`). The Agent tool only takes aliases.
- **Claude cost figures.** `total_cost_usd` from `claude -p` is Claude Code's own estimate, and its price table lags new models: it priced a Haiku 5.5 call at about 60 times the list price. On a subscription, runs use plan limits, not dollars. Each headless Claude call also loads about 20k to 45k tokens of setup, so many tiny Claude calls cost more than one batched call.
- **`--bare` breaks sign-in.** `claude --bare` skips the keychain, so OAuth (claude.ai) sign-in fails. The CLI does not use it.
- **Session protocol in workers.** Every harness loads global agent instructions (`AGENTS.md`, `CLAUDE.md`), and these may tell agents to claim tasks or log events. The worker preamble tells workers not to. Leave it on (do not pass `--raw`) for real work.
- **Codex model flag.** Codex's `spawn_agent` tells the model not to set `model` unless the user asks. /subagent is that ask.
- **Codex approvals.** Headless Codex runs with `approval_policy="never"`, so a blocked command fails back to the model instead of hanging.
- **OpenCode plan agent.** `--agent plan` blocks edits but may still ask for some shell commands; headless runs cannot answer, so those calls fail.
- **Ollama models.** A tier model must be pulled (`ollama list`). `subagent doctor` warns when it is not. Large models take a while to load on the first call.
- **Local models drift.** In the 2026-10-12 skill-list test, OpenCode on local qwen3-coder replied with a generic greeting instead of the answer. The run still counted as ok, because `ok` only means the harness returned text. Give local models narrow tasks with the input attached, and check every answer.
- **Models miscount lines in attached files.** In 2026-10-15 QA, files attached without line numbers led gpt-6-luna to get every line number wrong (often off by one) and qwen3-coder to be off too, while the same model reading the file with its own tools was right. `--attach` now numbers each line of a text file by default.
- **DeepSeek harness.** Headless dsh has no read-only mode and no model flag, so the CLI refuses it without `--allow-unsandboxed`. Check which provider and model its profile uses (`agent-default-model` in `~/.dsh/settings.yaml`) before you send it anything private, and run `subagent doctor --probe --include-unsandboxed` to confirm the model is still live: free preview models on OpenRouter are retired without notice.
